title: Budgeting your thinking time
summary: Spend time where it matters: fast routine moves, long thinks at critical moments, and a reserve for the end. Includes time-trouble technique.

steps.md:
Most club players lose time in two ways: **too fast** in critical positions (Heisman: improving players play too fast in slow games) and **too slow** on routine moves (re-checking the same line, Kotov's warning). A budget fixes both:

- Opening: quick, from preparation.
- Middlegame: most of your time, concentrated on **critical moments** (captures that change the structure, sacrifices, trades into an endgame, surprises).
- Reserve: enough for the last moves before the time control or the endgame.

Rule of thumb for classical games: no more than about a third of your time used by move 15 unless the position is critical.

steps.question: 90-minute game, no increment. It is move 12, a quiet position, and you have used 40 minutes. What is the best adjustment?
choices: Fine: the opening deserves the most time
You are behind schedule: play routine moves faster and save long thinks for genuinely critical moments
Start playing blitz moves for the rest of the game
Offer a draw to avoid time trouble
steps.explain: Forty minutes by move 12 is over the one-third guideline in a quiet position. Do not panic into blitz; just stop re-checking routine moves and keep the long thinks for critical moments.

steps.question: Which of these positions most deserves a long think?
choices: Recapturing a piece where only one recapture is legal
Deciding whether to trade queens into a pawn endgame
Playing your 6th move of a main-line opening you know
Moving your king out of a check with only one legal square
steps.explain: Transitions into pawn endgames are irreversible and often decided by a single tempo. Forced recaptures, only-moves and known theory should take seconds.

steps.prompt: Calm position, you are short of time. Spend your seconds on a safety check, then make a simple, solid move: develop the a1-rook to the centre.
steps.explain: In time trouble, prefer safe, useful moves that do not create new weaknesses. Rad1 connects the rooks and adds pressure on d6 without opening anything. Save calculation for forcing positions.
steps.hint: A rook move to a central file.

steps.question: You have 3 minutes left for 8 moves, no increment, in an unclear middlegame. What is the best practical approach?
choices: Calculate one long sacrificial line to the end
Simplify, make safe moves, and think on your opponent's time
Stop recording moves and ask the arbiter for extra time
Spend 2 minutes on the next move to get it right
steps.explain: Time-trouble technique: simplify, avoid long forcing lines you cannot verify, keep pieces protected, use the opponent's time. You may stop recording when under five minutes with less than 30 seconds increment (Art. 8.4).

steps.question: Your opponent is in severe time trouble and you are better. Which approach is most practical?
choices: Force a long series of exchanges so the position becomes simple
Keep the position complicated but safe, avoiding forcing simplifications
Offer a draw so they relax
Play as fast as possible yourself
steps.explain: Against a short clock, keep tension and problems on the board while keeping your own position safe. Forcing simplifications let a player in time trouble make easy, obvious moves.

steps.question: In a 90+30 game you have 2 minutes left. How should you treat the increment?
choices: Ignore it: it is too small to matter
Never let your clock fall below the level where the 30 seconds alone is enough for a safe move
Use the full 30 seconds plus a minute on every move
Play pre-moves to gain time
steps.explain: With increment, the danger is spending more than the increment on several moves in a row. Keep enough of a cushion so that each move can be checked for safety. Pre-moves do not exist over the board.

steps.question: Retrieval check: which statement best describes good time budgeting?
choices: Equal time for every move
Fast in the opening and on routine or forced moves, long thinks at critical moments, a reserve for the end
Always use half your time on the first ten moves
Spend most time in the endgame because it decides games
steps.explain: A budget is uneven by design: time follows criticality. Practise this in your training games and review where your minutes went afterwards.

sources: Kotov, Think Like a Grandmaster (time trouble)
